entities.name: Lucius Aelius Lamia
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Aelius Lamia, a prominent Roman Senator of the early Julio-Claudian era, distinguished himself as a reliable and high-ranking administrator from the reign of Augustus through Tiberius. Born into an ancient, though not patrician, family that had achieved senatorial rank, Lamia's career trajectory exemplifies the opportunities available to capable individuals within the evolving Roman Principate. His consulship in 3 CE, alongside Marcus Servilius, marked a pivotal point in his political ascent, solidifying his position within the imperial elite.

Over several decades, Lamia held a series of critical appointments that underscored his administrative competence and loyalty to the imperial house. Following his consulship, he served as proconsul of Africa, a wealthy and strategically vital province, overseeing its administration and financial affairs. Subsequently, he was appointed legate of Syria, a frontier province necessitating a firm hand and diplomatic skill due to its proximity to the Parthian Empire and diverse client kingdoms. His final major post was the prestigious and powerful Urban Prefecture of Rome, which he assumed in 32 CE and held until his death in 33 CE, a role that placed him in charge of the capital's order and essential services.

Lamia's career is a testament to the administrative stability sought by the early emperors and the continued importance of the senatorial class in providing competent governance across the vast Roman Empire. He represented the archetype of the imperial official who, while not an innovator or military conqueror, was instrumental in the daily functioning and consolidation of the Principate. His sons, notably Lucius Aelius Lamia Plautius Aelianus, continued the family's public service, demonstrating the establishment of a new aristocratic lineage rooted in imperial favor and administrative prowess.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lucius Aelius Lamia was a high-ranking Roman senator and administrator whose career spanning the reigns of Augustus and Tiberius provided crucial stability to the early Principate by governing key provinces and the capital itself. His diligent service contributed to the consolidation of imperial power and exemplified the ongoing importance of the senatorial class in Roman governance.
